rooms.about: A survey of British literature from Old English epic to the modern novel, paired with the reading, research and essay-writing skills expected in a first-year college course.

units.t: Old English and the Epic: Beowulf
learn: Old English was the language of the Anglo-Saxons, who settled in Britain from about 450 CE. It looks foreign to modern readers because it was heavily Germanic and had many word endings that later disappeared. Beowulf, written down around 1000 CE, is the longest surviving Old English poem at about 3,182 lines.

Beowulf is an epic: a long narrative poem about a hero whose deeds matter to a whole people. Beowulf fights three monsters: Grendel, Grendel’s mother and, fifty years later, a dragon. The poem asks what makes a good warrior and a good king, and it mixes older pagan values with Christian ideas added by the scribe.

Old English poetry uses alliteration rather than rhyme. Each line has two halves split by a pause called a caesura, and stressed words in both halves begin with the same sound. Poets also used kennings, compressed metaphors such as “whale-road” for the sea or “bone-house” for the body.

Key values in the poem include loyalty between a lord and his warriors (the comitatus bond), fame earned through brave deeds, and generosity, shown when a king shares treasure. The poem is also elegiac: it mourns how all glory fades, ending with Beowulf’s funeral and fears for his people’s future.
units.try: Write four lines of your own Old English–style verse about a modern challenge, such as an exam. Put a pause (caesura) in the middle of each line, make at least two stressed words in each line alliterate, and invent two kennings, for example “screen-glow” for a phone or “thought-trial” for a test.
check: What sound device does Old English poetry mainly use?
A compressed metaphor like “whale-road” for sea
A rhyming couplet that ends a poem
A speech given by a king

learn: After the Norman Conquest of 1066, French became the language of England’s ruling class. Over three centuries English absorbed thousands of French words and lost most of its old endings, becoming Middle English. Geoffrey Chaucer, writing in the late 1300s, helped prove English could be a language of serious literature.

The Canterbury Tales is a frame narrative: an outer story holds many inner stories. About thirty pilgrims travel to the shrine at Canterbury and agree to a storytelling contest. The General Prologue introduces them, from the noble Knight to the corrupt Pardoner, giving a cross-section of medieval society.

Chaucer is a master of satire, using humor to expose faults. He often lets characters condemn themselves: the Pardoner openly admits he preaches against greed while selling fake relics for profit. This is irony, a gap between what is said or expected and what is true.

Chaucer wrote mostly in iambic pentameter rhyming couplets, lines of ten syllables alternating unstressed and stressed beats, rhymed in pairs. The Wife of Bath’s Tale raises the question of what women most desire, and her answer, control over their own lives, still sparks debate.
units.try: Write a short “General Prologue” portrait, 6 to 8 lines, of a modern traveler (for example a social media influencer or a sports fan on a bus trip). Use gentle satire: let one detail quietly reveal a flaw, the way Chaucer’s narrator praises characters while exposing them.
check: An outer story that contains other stories
A poem with exactly fourteen lines
A story told only through letters
Why were the pilgrims in The Canterbury Tales traveling?
To visit the shrine at Canterbury
To fight in a war in France

learn: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote about 37 plays and 154 sonnets during the English Renaissance. A tragedy shows a person of high rank brought to ruin, often through a tragic flaw, or hamartia. In Macbeth, a brave Scottish general is undone by ambition after three witches predict he will be king.

Shakespeare writes most noble speech in blank verse, unrhymed iambic pentameter, and uses prose for lower characters or madness. A soliloquy is a speech given alone on stage that reveals a character’s thoughts, such as Macbeth’s “Is this a dagger which I see before me.”

Major themes in Macbeth include unchecked ambition, guilt and the disruption of natural order. Imagery of blood, darkness and sleep runs through the play. Lady Macbeth, at first the stronger of the two, later sleepwalks and tries to wash imaginary blood from her hands.

Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something a character does not. When King Duncan praises Macbeth’s castle as pleasant, we already know Macbeth plans to murder him there. Watching for these moments helps you see how Shakespeare builds suspense.
units.try: Pick one short soliloquy from Macbeth. Read it aloud twice, tapping the five stressed beats in each line. Then rewrite it in plain modern English in four sentences and note one image (blood, darkness or sleep) that the original uses but your version loses.
check: A speech alone on stage revealing a character’s thoughts
A song sung by the chorus
Too much trust in his children

learn: The sonnet is a 14-line poem in iambic pentameter. The Shakespearean sonnet has three quatrains and a final couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. The couplet often delivers a twist or conclusion, called the volta or turn, though the turn can also come earlier.

In the early 1600s, the Metaphysical poets, including John Donne and Andrew Marvell, wrote witty, argumentative poems. They used conceits, extended and surprising comparisons. Donne compares two separated lovers to the legs of a drawing compass: one stays fixed while the other circles, yet they remain joined.

Marvell’s “To His Coy Mistress” uses a three-part argument: if we had endless time, I would court you slowly; but time is short; therefore, let us act now. This carpe diem, or “seize the day,” theme appears across Renaissance poetry.

John Milton’s Paradise Lost (1667) is an epic in blank verse of over 10,000 lines retelling the fall of humankind. Its Satan is so persuasive that readers still debate whether Milton made him too heroic.
units.try: Write your own conceit: compare a friendship to an unexpected object (a phone charger, a bridge, a library card) and extend the comparison for at least five lines, showing three different ways the two things are alike.
check: How many lines does a sonnet have?
A list of a poet’s influences

learn: The 1700s Enlightenment valued reason, order and social improvement. Writers often used satire to criticize society. Satire can be Horatian, gentle and amused, or Juvenalian, harsh and angry.

Jonathan Swift’s “A Modest Proposal” (1729) is a famous Juvenalian satire. Writing as a calm economist, Swift suggests that poor Irish families sell their babies as food to the rich. The shocking idea exposes how cruelly English policy treated the Irish poor. Its power comes from verbal irony: Swift means the opposite of what he says.

Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels (1726) sends a ship’s surgeon to strange lands, such as Lilliput, where tiny people go to war over which end to crack an egg. The point is that human politics can be just as petty.

Alexander Pope wrote in heroic couplets, rhymed pairs of iambic pentameter lines. The Rape of the Lock is a mock-epic: it treats a trivial event, the cutting of a lock of hair, with grand epic style to mock high society’s vanity.
units.try: Choose a small, real annoyance (long lunch lines, group chat drama) and write a one-paragraph mock-epic description of it, using grand, heroic language to show how silly the situation is. Then write one sentence explaining what your satire criticizes.
check: What does “A Modest Proposal” use to make its point?
Verbal irony: Swift means the opposite of what he says
A love story set in Ireland
A work that treats a trivial subject in grand epic style
A true epic that was lost and rewritten
A play mocking a real king by name

learn: The Romantic period ran roughly from 1798 to 1832. Reacting against Enlightenment reason and industrial cities, Romantics valued emotion, imagination, nature and the individual. William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge launched the movement with Lyrical Ballads in 1798.

Wordsworth defined poetry as “the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings” recollected in tranquility. He wrote in everyday language about ordinary people and nature, as in “I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud,” where remembering daffodils later fills his heart with pleasure.

The second generation included Lord Byron, Percy Shelley and John Keats. Shelley’s “Ozymandias” shows a shattered statue of a proud king in the desert, a lesson about how power fades. Keats’s odes, such as “Ode to a Nightingale,” explore beauty, death and imagination.

Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818) is a Romantic and Gothic novel often called the first science fiction story. Victor Frankenstein creates life and then abandons his creature, raising questions about responsibility, ambition and what makes someone a monster.
units.try: Spend ten minutes outdoors or at a window observing one natural thing closely. Write notes on what you see, hear and feel. Later that day, write an eight-line poem from memory, as Wordsworth did, and compare what you remembered with your notes.
check: Which collection launched English Romanticism in 1798?
Human power and pride do not last

learn: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901, a time of industry, empire, scientific change and social inequality. Many Victorian writers explored duty, class, faith and progress. The novel became the most popular literary form, often published in monthly parts.

Charles Dickens exposed poverty, child labor and debtors’ prisons in novels like Oliver Twist and Great Expectations. In Great Expectations, the orphan Pip learns that wealth and status do not make a gentleman; loyalty and kindness do.

Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre (1847) follows a poor, independent governess who insists on her own worth. Emily Brontë’s Wuthering Heights is a stormy tale of passion and revenge. Both are told by first-person narrators whose reliability readers should question.

Victorian poets include Alfred, Lord Tennyson and Robert Browning. Browning perfected the dramatic monologue, a poem spoken by one character to a silent listener. In “My Last Duchess,” a duke reveals, without meaning to, that he had his wife killed.
units.try: Write a short dramatic monologue (10 to 14 lines) in which a speaker talks to a silent listener and accidentally reveals something they would rather hide. Have a friend read it and tell you what they figured out about the speaker.
check: A poem spoken by one character to a silent listener
A play with only one act
What does Pip learn in Great Expectations?
Loyalty and kindness matter more than wealth

learn: Modernism (about 1900–1945) responded to World War I, new technology and doubts about old certainties. Modernist writers broke traditional forms, using fragments, multiple viewpoints and stream of consciousness, which imitates the flow of a character’s thoughts.

Virginia Woolf’s Mrs. Dalloway (1925) takes place over a single day in London, moving between the minds of characters. James Joyce’s Ulysses also covers one day, in Dublin. T. S. Eliot’s poem The Waste Land (1922) mixes voices and languages to capture a broken postwar culture.

World War I poets such as Wilfred Owen described the horror of trench warfare. Owen’s “Dulce et Decorum Est” attacks the old saying that it is sweet to die for your country, describing a gas attack in vivid, painful detail.

After 1945, British literature reflected the end of empire and new voices. George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) warns about totalitarian control of truth and language, introducing terms like “Big Brother” and “doublethink.”
units.try: Write a 200-word stream-of-consciousness passage covering one minute of your morning. Let your thoughts jump between what you see, memories and worries without neat transitions. Then underline three places where one thought triggers the next.
check: Writing that imitates the flow of a character’s thoughts
What does Nineteen Eighty-Four warn about?
Totalitarian control of truth and language

learn: A strong academic essay has a clear thesis, a one- or two-sentence claim that is arguable and specific. “Frankenstein is about science” is weak. “Frankenstein argues that the true monster is the creator who abandons responsibility” is arguable and gives the essay direction.

Each body paragraph should follow a pattern: a topic sentence linked to the thesis, evidence such as a quotation, analysis that explains how the evidence supports the claim, and a link back to the thesis. Analysis should be longer than the quotation.

Good arguments address counterarguments. Acknowledge a reasonable opposing view, then explain why your claim still holds. This shows fairness and builds ethos, your credibility. Arguments also use logos (logic and evidence) and pathos (appeals to emotion).

For a personal college admissions essay, focus on a specific moment rather than a list of achievements. Show growth or reflection, use concrete details, and write in your own voice. Most prompts allow around 650 words.
units.try: Take a novel or poem from this course and write a thesis statement for it. Test it with three questions: Could someone reasonably disagree? Is it specific? Can I support it with at least three pieces of evidence? Revise until all three answers are yes.
check: It asks a question with no answer
An appeal based on the writer’s credibility

learn: A research paper begins with a focused question. Find sources, then evaluate them for credibility: Who wrote it? What are their qualifications? Is it current? Is it biased? Primary sources are original materials; secondary sources analyze them.

You can use a source by quoting (exact words in quotation marks), paraphrasing (restating an idea fully in your own words) or summarizing (giving the main points briefly). All three require citation. Presenting others’ ideas or words as your own is plagiarism, a serious academic offense.

English classes usually use MLA style. An in-text citation gives the author’s last name and page number in parentheses, such as (Woolf 42). A Works Cited page at the end lists full details for every source, in alphabetical order by author.

Before submitting, revise for argument and organization first, then edit sentences, then proofread for spelling and punctuation. Reading your paper aloud is one of the best ways to catch errors and awkward phrasing.
units.try: Choose one paragraph from an article about a book you studied. Write a direct quotation with an MLA in-text citation, a paraphrase of the same idea in your own words, and a one-sentence summary. Compare the three and check that your paraphrase does not copy the original’s sentence structure.
check: What does an MLA in-text citation usually include?
The author’s last name and page number
The date you read the source
Which uses of a source require citation?

rooms.about: Functions, trigonometry, sequences and limits to prepare for calculus, followed by the core ideas of statistics: describing data, probability, distributions and inference.

learn: A function assigns exactly one output to each input. The domain is the set of allowed inputs and the range is the set of outputs. For f(x) = √(x − 2), the domain is x ≥ 2 because you cannot take the square root of a negative real number.

Transformations move a parent graph. For y = a·f(x − h) + k, the graph shifts right h units and up k units. If |a| > 1 it stretches vertically; if 0 < |a| < 1 it compresses; if a is negative it reflects over the x-axis.
Composition means plugging one function into another: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)). If f(x) = x² and g(x) = x + 3, then f(g(x)) = (x + 3)², while g(f(x)) = x² + 3. Order matters.

An inverse function undoes the original. To find it, swap x and y and solve for y. If f(x) = 2x + 6, then f⁻¹(x) = (x − 6)/2. A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one, passing the horizontal line test.
units.try: Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x − 1)/4. Step 1: write y = (3x − 1)/4. Step 2: swap: x = (3y − 1)/4. Step 3: multiply by 4: 4x = 3y − 1. Step 4: add 1: 4x + 1 = 3y. Step 5: divide by 3: f⁻¹(x) = (4x + 1)/3. Check: f(1) = 0.5 and f⁻¹(0.5) = (2 + 1)/3 = 1.
check: What is the domain of f(x) = √(x − 5)?
If f(x) = x² and g(x) = x + 1, what is f(g(2))?

learn: A polynomial of degree n has at most n real zeros and at most n − 1 turning points. End behavior depends on the leading term: for y = −2x³, the graph rises to the left and falls to the right.

Zeros can be found by factoring. If p(x) = x³ − 4x = x(x − 2)(x + 2), the zeros are 0, 2 and −2. The Rational Root Theorem says any rational zero is a factor of the constant term divided by a factor of the leading coefficient.

A rational function is a ratio of polynomials, like r(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 3). A vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not: here x = 3. If a factor cancels from top and bottom, there is a hole instead.
Horizontal asymptotes depend on degrees. If the top degree is less than the bottom, y = 0. If equal, y = ratio of leading coefficients. For r(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 3), degrees are equal, so y = 1/1 = 1.
units.try: Analyze r(x) = (2x² − 8)/(x² − x − 6). Factor: top 2(x − 2)(x + 2), bottom (x − 3)(x + 2). The factor (x + 2) cancels, so there is a hole at x = −2. Vertical asymptote: x = 3. Degrees are equal, so the horizontal asymptote is y = 2/1 = 2. Zero: x = 2.
check: What is the vertical asymptote of y = 5/(x + 4)?
What is the maximum number of real zeros of a degree-5 polynomial?

learn: An exponential function has the form f(x) = a·bˣ. If b > 1 it shows growth; if 0 < b < 1, decay. Compound interest uses A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ, and continuous growth uses A = Peʳᵗ, where e ≈ 2.718.
A logarithm is an exponent: log_b(x) = y means bʸ = x. So log₂(8) = 3 because 2³ = 8. The common log uses base 10 and the natural log, ln, uses base e.
Log rules: log(MN) = log M + log N; log(M/N) = log M − log N; log(Mᵖ) = p·log M. The change-of-base formula is log_b(x) = ln x / ln b.

To solve an exponential equation, take a log of both sides. To solve 3ˣ = 20, write x = ln 20 / ln 3 ≈ 2.727. Always check that a log’s input is positive, since logs of zero or negatives are undefined.
units.try: How long does $1,000 take to double at 5% interest compounded continuously? Step 1: 2000 = 1000e^(0.05t). Step 2: divide: 2 = e^(0.05t). Step 3: take ln: ln 2 = 0.05t. Step 4: t = 0.6931/0.05 ≈ 13.9 years.

units.t: Trigonometric Functions and the Unit Circle
learn: Angles can be measured in radians. One full turn is 360° or 2π radians, so π radians = 180°. To convert degrees to radians, multiply by π/180: 60° = π/3.
The unit circle has radius 1. For an angle θ, the point on the circle is (cos θ, sin θ). Key values: at π/6, (√3/2, 1/2); at π/4, (√2/2, √2/2); at π/3, (1/2, √3/2). Tangent is sin θ / cos θ.

Sine and cosine graphs are periodic with period 2π and amplitude 1. In y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D, |A| is the amplitude, 2π/|B| is the period, C is the phase shift and D is the vertical shift (the midline).
Sinusoidal functions model repeating patterns such as tides, daylight hours and sound waves. If a tide ranges from 2 m to 8 m every 12 hours, its amplitude is 3, midline 5 and B = 2π/12 = π/6.
units.try: Find the amplitude, period and midline of y = 4 sin(2x) − 1. Amplitude: |4| = 4. Period: 2π/2 = π. Midline: y = −1. So the graph oscillates between −1 + 4 = 3 and −1 − 4 = −5, completing one cycle every π units.
check: What is the period of y = sin(3x)?

learn: The Pythagorean identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 comes straight from the unit circle, where x² + y² = 1. Dividing by cos²θ gives 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ.
Other key identities: double angle sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ. Sum formulas: sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B.
To verify an identity, work on one side only, rewriting it until it matches the other. Converting everything to sine and cosine is often a good first step.

To solve a trig equation, isolate the trig function, then find all angles. sin x = 1/2 gives x = π/6 and 5π/6 in [0, 2π). Because trig functions repeat, the general solutions add 2πn for any integer n.
units.try: Solve 2cos²x − 1 = 0 on [0, 2π). Step 1: cos²x = 1/2. Step 2: cos x = ±√2/2. Step 3: cos x = √2/2 at π/4 and 7π/4; cos x = −√2/2 at 3π/4 and 5π/4. So x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4.

units.t: Sequences, Series and an Introduction to Limits
learn: An arithmetic sequence adds a common difference d: aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d. A geometric sequence multiplies by a common ratio r: aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹. In 3, 6, 12, 24, r = 2.

A series is a sum of terms. An arithmetic series of n terms sums to n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. A finite geometric series sums to a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). If |r| < 1, an infinite geometric series converges to a₁/(1 − r).
A limit describes the value a function approaches as x approaches a number. For f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1), f(1) is undefined, but factoring gives x + 1, so the limit as x → 1 is 2.
Limits are the foundation of calculus. They define instantaneous rate of change: the slope of a curve at a point is the limit of slopes of secant lines as the two points move together.
units.try: Find the sum of the infinite series 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + … Step 1: a₁ = 8, r = 4/8 = 1/2. Step 2: |r| < 1, so it converges. Step 3: sum = 8/(1 − 1/2) = 8/(1/2) = 16.
check: What is the common ratio of 5, 15, 45, 135?
What is the limit of (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x → 2?

learn: Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing and interpreting data. Categorical variables place individuals in groups (eye color); quantitative variables are numbers (height). Choose graphs to match: bar charts for categorical, histograms and box plots for quantitative.

Describe a distribution by its shape, center, spread and unusual features. Shape may be symmetric, skewed right (long tail to the right) or skewed left. In right-skewed data, the mean is usually greater than the median.
The median and interquartile range (IQR = Q3 − Q1) are resistant to outliers. The mean and standard deviation are not. A common rule flags outliers below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR.

Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean. A z-score tells how many standard deviations a value is from the mean: z = (x − mean)/SD. A score of 85 when the mean is 75 and SD is 5 has z = 2.
units.try: Data: 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 9, 30. Median = 5. Q1 = 4, Q3 = 9, so IQR = 5. Upper fence: 9 + 1.5(5) = 16.5. Since 30 > 16.5, it is an outlier. Mean = 61/7 ≈ 8.7, pulled above the median by the outlier.
check: Which measure of center resists outliers?
A value has z = −1.5. What does that mean?
It is 1.5 standard deviations below the mean
It is 1.5 points below the mean

learn: Probability measures how likely an event is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). For equally likely outcomes, P(A) = favorable outcomes / total outcomes. The complement rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
The addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Subtracting avoids counting overlap twice. If events are mutually exclusive (cannot both happen), P(A and B) = 0.
Conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B), the chance of A given B happened. Events are independent if P(A | B) = P(A). For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B).
Counting helps: the number of ways to arrange n objects is n!. Choosing r from n where order does not matter is the combination nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). For 5 choose 2, that is 10.
units.try: A bag holds 4 red and 6 blue marbles. Draw two without replacement. P(both red) = (4/10)·(3/9) = 12/90 = 2/15 ≈ 0.133. Notice the second fraction changes because one red marble is gone, so the draws are not independent.
check: If P(A) = 0.3, what is P(not A)?
For independent events with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4, what is P(A and B)?

learn: A normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped curve described by its mean μ and standard deviation σ. The empirical rule says about 68% of values fall within 1σ of the mean, 95% within 2σ and 99.7% within 3σ.
To find probabilities, convert to a z-score and use a table or calculator. If test scores are normal with μ = 500 and σ = 100, a score of 700 has z = 2, so about 97.5% of scores are below it.

A sample is a part of a population. A simple random sample gives every group of individuals an equal chance of selection, reducing bias. Convenience samples and voluntary response samples often produce biased results.

Sample statistics vary from sample to sample. The sampling distribution of a sample mean has the same center as the population, but its spread shrinks as sample size grows: σ/√n. Larger samples give more precise estimates.
units.try: Heights are normal with μ = 66 inches and σ = 3. What percent are between 60 and 72 inches? Step 1: 60 is 2σ below; 72 is 2σ above. Step 2: by the empirical rule, about 95% fall within 2σ. Answer: about 95%.
check: About what percent of normal data lies within 1 standard deviation of the mean?
Why is a simple random sample preferred?
It is always the largest sample

learn: A confidence interval estimates a population value: estimate ± margin of error. A 95% confidence level means that if we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of such intervals would capture the true value.

A significance test checks a claim. Start with a null hypothesis (no effect) and an alternative. The p-value is the probability of results at least as extreme as ours if the null is true. A small p-value, often below 0.05, is evidence against the null.

For two quantitative variables, a scatterplot shows form, direction and strength. The correlation r ranges from −1 to 1; values near ±1 mean a strong linear relationship. Correlation does not prove causation.
The least-squares regression line ŷ = a + bx predicts y from x. The slope b is the predicted change in y for each one-unit increase in x. A residual is actual y minus predicted ŷ.
units.try: A regression line for study hours (x) and test score (y) is ŷ = 62 + 4x. Predict the score for 5 hours: 62 + 4(5) = 82. If a student who studied 5 hours scored 78, the residual is 78 − 82 = −4, meaning the model over-predicted by 4 points.
check: What does a small p-value suggest?
The null hypothesis is proven true
A correlation of r = −0.9 indicates what?

rooms.about: How Earth’s systems work, from plate tectonics and rocks to the atmosphere, oceans and climate, and how human use of resources affects ecosystems and our shared future.

learn: Scientists study Earth as four connected spheres: the geosphere (rock and soil), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (living things). Some also add the cryosphere, Earth’s ice. A change in one sphere affects the others.

Energy drives Earth’s systems. Sunlight powers weather, ocean currents and photosynthesis. Heat from Earth’s interior, left over from its formation and produced by radioactive decay, drives plate motion and volcanoes.

Matter cycles through the spheres. In the carbon cycle, carbon moves from the atmosphere into plants by photosynthesis, into animals that eat plants, into soil and oceans, and back to the air through respiration, decay, volcanoes and burning fuels.

Feedback loops change how systems respond. A positive feedback amplifies change: melting ice exposes darker ocean that absorbs more heat, causing more melting. A negative feedback dampens change and helps keep a system stable.
units.try: Pick one event, such as a volcanic eruption. Draw four circles labeled geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere. Draw arrows showing at least five effects, for example ash entering the atmosphere, which blocks sunlight, which cools temperatures, which affects crops.
check: Which sphere includes all living things?
What does a positive feedback loop do?

learn: Earth’s rigid outer shell, the lithosphere, is broken into about a dozen large plates and many small ones. They move a few centimeters per year, about as fast as fingernails grow, riding on the hotter, slowly flowing asthenosphere beneath.

At divergent boundaries, plates move apart and new crust forms, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. At convergent boundaries, plates collide: dense ocean crust sinks beneath another plate in subduction, forming trenches and volcanoes, while two continents crumple into mountains like the Himalayas.
At transform boundaries, plates slide past each other sideways, as along the San Andreas Fault in California. Stress builds until rocks slip suddenly, releasing energy as an earthquake.

Evidence for plate tectonics includes matching fossils and rocks on separate continents, the fit of coastlines like South America and Africa, magnetic stripes on the seafloor that are symmetric around ridges, and seafloor rock that gets older farther from ridges.
units.try: Use a world map. Mark where you know major earthquakes or volcanoes occur, such as Japan, Chile, Iceland and Indonesia. Then compare with a plate boundary map. Notice the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” where about 75% of active volcanoes lie along subduction zones.
check: What happens at a divergent boundary?
Plates move apart and new crust forms
What type of boundary is the San Andreas Fault?

units.t: Rocks, Minerals and the Rock Cycle
learn: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical makeup and crystal structure. Quartz, feldspar and calcite are common. Minerals are identified by hardness (Mohs scale 1–10), luster, streak, cleavage and other properties.
Rocks are made of minerals. Igneous rocks form when magma or lava cools: slow cooling underground makes large crystals (granite); fast cooling at the surface makes small crystals (basalt).

Sedimentary rocks form when sediments are deposited, compacted and cemented, as in sandstone and limestone. They often contain fossils and form layers. Metamorphic rocks form when heat and pressure change existing rock without melting it: shale becomes slate and limestone becomes marble.
The rock cycle links all three. Any rock can be weathered into sediment, buried and changed by heat and pressure, or melted into magma. These processes usually take thousands to millions of years.
units.try: Collect five small rocks from a yard or park (only where collecting is allowed). Look at each with a magnifier. Note crystal size, layers, grains or fossils, and try a scratch test with a steel nail (hardness about 5.5). Guess whether each is igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic and explain why.
check: How does granite get its large crystals?
Lava cools quickly at the surface
Marble is metamorphic rock formed from what?

learn: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. Geologists divide this into eons, eras, periods and epochs. Most of Earth’s history was the Precambrian; complex animals became common only in the last 540 million years or so.

Relative dating orders events. The law of superposition says that in undisturbed layers, lower rocks are older. A fault or intrusion is younger than the layers it cuts through. Index fossils of widespread, short-lived species help match layers across regions.

Absolute dating gives ages in years using radioactive decay. Each isotope has a half-life, the time for half of it to decay. If a mineral has 25% of its original parent isotope left, two half-lives have passed.

Life has seen at least five mass extinctions. The most famous, about 66 million years ago, ended the non-avian dinosaurs and is linked to an asteroid impact. The largest, about 252 million years ago, wiped out roughly 90% of marine species.
units.try: Make a geologic time scale on a 4.6-meter strip of paper or string, where 1 meter equals 1 billion years. Mark Earth’s formation, first life (about 3.8 billion years ago), first land plants (about 470 million years ago), dinosaurs’ end and humans (about 300,000 years ago, under a millimeter from the end).
check: In undisturbed rock layers, which are oldest?
After two half-lives, how much parent isotope remains?

learn: The atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapor. Its layers are the troposphere (where weather happens), stratosphere (containing the ozone layer), mesosphere and thermosphere.

Uneven heating by the Sun drives weather. Warm air rises and cools, and its water vapor condenses into clouds. Air moves from high pressure to low pressure, creating wind. Earth’s rotation curves winds by the Coriolis effect.
An air mass is a large body of air with similar temperature and humidity. Where two meet, a front forms. A cold front often brings brief, intense storms; a warm front brings longer, gentler rain.

Severe weather includes thunderstorms, tornadoes and hurricanes. Hurricanes form over warm ocean water, at least about 26°C (79°F), and draw energy from evaporating water. Forecasters use satellites, radar and computer models.
units.try: For one week, record the temperature, sky conditions, wind and air pressure (from a weather report) each day at the same time. Look for patterns: does pressure drop before rain? Write a short forecast for the next day based on your data, then check how you did.
check: In which layer does most weather occur?
Air generally moves from where to where?

learn: Oceans cover about 71% of Earth’s surface and hold about 97% of its water. Only about 3% of water is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice caps and glaciers or stored underground.

In the water cycle, water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and returns to oceans by runoff or soaks into the ground as groundwater. An aquifer is an underground layer of rock or sediment that holds usable water.

Surface ocean currents are driven by wind and bend because of the Coriolis effect. Deep currents form a global conveyor belt driven by differences in temperature and salt, called thermohaline circulation. The Gulf Stream carries warm water that keeps western Europe milder.

Oceans absorb a large share of the extra heat and carbon dioxide humans add. Absorbed CO₂ forms carbonic acid, lowering ocean pH. This ocean acidification makes it harder for corals and shellfish to build shells.
units.try: Make a model of density currents. Fill a clear container with room-temperature water. Gently pour in a small cup of very cold, salty water with a few drops of food coloring along the side. Watch it sink and spread along the bottom, like deep ocean currents.
check: About what percent of Earth’s water is fresh?
Differences in temperature and salt content

learn: Weather is short-term conditions; climate is the average pattern over 30 years or more. Climate depends on latitude, elevation, nearness to oceans, ocean currents and prevailing winds.

The greenhouse effect keeps Earth livable. Gases like carbon dioxide, methane and water vapor absorb heat radiated from Earth’s surface and send some back down. Without it, Earth would average about −18°C instead of about 15°C.

Since the 1800s, burning fossil fuels and clearing forests have raised atmospheric CO₂ from about 280 parts per million to over 420 ppm. Global average temperature has risen by about 1.1–1.2°C, with effects including rising seas, melting glaciers and more intense heat waves.

Evidence comes from thermometers, satellites, ice cores that trap ancient air bubbles, tree rings and sediment. Responses include mitigation, reducing emissions, and adaptation, preparing for changes already happening.
units.try: Find average monthly temperatures for your town and a city at a very different latitude. Make a line graph of both. Explain two reasons their climates differ, using latitude, elevation or distance from the ocean.
check: What is the difference between weather and climate?
Weather is short-term; climate is the long-term average
What does the greenhouse effect do?

learn: An ecosystem includes living things and their physical environment. Energy flows from producers (plants, algae) to consumers to decomposers. Only about 10% of energy passes to each higher level of a food chain; the rest is used or lost as heat.

Biomes are large regions with similar climate and life, such as tropical rainforest, desert, grassland, tundra, and deciduous and coniferous forest. Rainforests cover about 6% of land but hold over half of land species.

Biodiversity is the variety of life: genetic, species and ecosystem diversity. Diverse ecosystems are more resilient. Keystone species, such as sea otters that control sea urchins and protect kelp forests, have outsized effects.

Major threats to biodiversity include habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, climate change and overharvesting. Ecological succession is how communities rebuild after a disturbance, from pioneer species like lichens to a mature community.
units.try: Do a 15-minute biodiversity survey in a small area such as a yard or park. Mark a 1-meter square and count different kinds of plants, insects and other organisms. Compare it with a second square, such as a mowed lawn versus an unmowed edge, and explain the difference.
check: About how much energy passes to the next level in a food chain?
A species with a large effect on its ecosystem
The largest animal in a habitat
A species found only on islands

learn: Renewable resources, such as sunlight, wind and forests, can be replaced naturally in a human lifetime if managed well. Nonrenewable resources, such as coal, oil, natural gas and minerals, form over millions of years.

Fossil fuels formed from ancient organisms buried and changed by heat and pressure. They are energy-dense and reliable but release CO₂ and other pollutants. Nuclear power produces almost no CO₂ but creates radioactive waste that must be stored safely.

Renewable sources include solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal and biomass. Their costs have fallen sharply, and solar and wind are now among the cheapest new electricity in many places, though they vary with weather and need storage or backup.
Soil is also a vital resource. It can take hundreds of years to form 2–3 centimeters. Practices such as cover crops, crop rotation and no-till farming reduce erosion and keep soil healthy.
units.try: Do a home energy audit. List ten devices you use daily, estimate hours of use, and look up or read their wattage. Calculate kilowatt-hours: watts × hours ÷ 1000. Identify the top three energy users and one change that could save energy.
check: What is a drawback of nuclear power?
It releases large amounts of CO₂

learn: Air pollution includes particulates, ozone at ground level and sulfur dioxide, which can form acid rain. The 1970 Clean Air Act in the United States greatly reduced many pollutants. Water pollution can come from point sources, like a factory pipe, or nonpoint sources, like fertilizer runoff from many farms.
Excess fertilizer can cause algae blooms that use up oxygen when they decay, creating dead zones. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone often covers several thousand square miles each summer.
Natural hazards include earthquakes, floods, wildfires, landslides and hurricanes. Hazard maps, building codes, early-warning systems and family emergency plans reduce harm.

Sustainability means meeting present needs without harming future generations’ ability to meet theirs. Strategies include reducing waste, reusing and recycling, protecting watersheds, improving efficiency and designing cities for walking and transit.
units.try: Track your household trash for three days, sorting it into landfill, recycling, compost and reusable. Weigh or estimate each. Make a plan to cut landfill waste by 25% and try it for a week.
check: Fertilizer runoff from many farms is an example of what?
Meeting present needs without harming future generations
Using resources as fast as possible

rooms.about: Core ideas of microeconomics and macroeconomics, from scarcity and markets to inflation and trade, plus the practical money skills of budgeting, banking, credit, investing and protecting yourself.

learn: Economics studies how people and societies use limited resources to meet unlimited wants. Because resources are scarce, every choice involves a trade-off. The four factors of production are land (natural resources), labor, capital (tools and buildings) and entrepreneurship.

Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative you give up. If you spend Saturday working a shift for $90 instead of studying, the lost study time is the opportunity cost of working; if you study, the $90 is.

A production possibilities frontier (PPF) shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can make. Points on the curve are efficient, points inside are underused, and points outside are impossible with current resources. Growth shifts the curve outward.
Economists assume people respond to incentives, rewards or penalties that change behavior. Thinking at the margin means comparing the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost.
units.try: List three choices you made this week, such as how you spent an evening or $20. For each, write the next-best alternative you gave up. Then decide whether the benefit was worth the opportunity cost and what you might choose differently.
check: The value of the next-best alternative given up
The price printed on an item
A point outside a PPF means what?
It cannot be reached with current resources

learn: The law of demand says that as price rises, the quantity demanded falls, all else equal. The law of supply says that as price rises, producers supply more. On a graph, demand slopes down and supply slopes up.

Equilibrium is where the curves cross: quantity supplied equals quantity demanded. If price is above equilibrium, a surplus results; below, a shortage. Markets tend to move toward equilibrium as sellers adjust prices.

A change in price moves along a curve. A change in other factors shifts the whole curve. Demand shifts with income, tastes, prices of related goods and expectations. Supply shifts with input costs, technology and the number of sellers.

Price controls set limits. A price ceiling, a legal maximum such as rent control, can cause shortages if set below equilibrium. A price floor, a legal minimum such as a minimum wage, can cause surpluses if set above equilibrium. Economists debate the size of these effects.
units.try: Imagine a new study finds that blueberries improve memory. Sketch supply and demand for blueberries. Which curve shifts, and which way? Then add a frost that destroys part of the crop. Predict what happens to price and explain each step.
check: If price is set below equilibrium, what results?
A change in the good’s own price

learn: Businesses may be sole proprietorships (one owner, unlimited personal liability), partnerships (two or more owners) or corporations (separate legal entities owned by shareholders, with limited liability). LLCs combine limited liability with simpler taxes.

Market structures range from perfect competition, with many sellers of identical products, to monopoly, with a single seller. Monopolistic competition has many sellers of slightly different products, like restaurants. An oligopoly has a few large firms, like airlines.
Firms aim to maximize profit: total revenue minus total cost. Costs are fixed (rent) or variable (materials). Firms produce up to the point where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

Government regulates markets to protect competition and consumers. Antitrust laws, starting with the Sherman Act of 1890, limit monopolies and price-fixing. Governments also address externalities, costs or benefits that fall on people outside a transaction, like pollution.
units.try: Plan a small business, like a dog-walking service. List fixed costs (leashes, flyers) and variable costs per walk. Set a price, then calculate how many walks you need each month to break even: fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per walk).
check: Which business structure gives owners limited liability?
A cost or benefit affecting people outside a transaction

learn: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year. It can be calculated as consumer spending + business investment + government purchases + net exports (C + I + G + NX).

Real GDP adjusts for inflation, so it shows changes in actual output. GDP per capita divides by population to compare living standards. GDP does not count unpaid work, leisure or environmental damage.

The unemployment rate is the share of the labor force without a job and actively looking. Types include frictional (between jobs), structural (skills do not match jobs) and cyclical (caused by recessions).

Inflation is a general rise in prices, often measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI). If the CPI rises from 300 to 309, inflation is 3%. Business cycles move through expansion, peak, contraction (recession) and trough.
units.try: Calculate inflation: a basket of goods cost $250 last year and $262.50 this year. Step 1: change = 262.50 − 250 = 12.50. Step 2: 12.50 ÷ 250 = 0.05. Inflation = 5%. If your pay rose 3%, your real wage fell about 2%.
check: The value of all final goods and services produced
The total money in bank accounts
Unemployment caused by a recession is called what?

learn: Money serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value. Banks keep only part of deposits on hand and lend the rest, which expands the money supply. This is called fractional reserve banking.

The Federal Reserve, or Fed, is the US central bank, created in 1913. It supervises banks, keeps the payment system running and conducts monetary policy aiming for maximum employment and stable prices, around 2% inflation.

The Fed’s main tool is setting a target for the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. Raising rates makes borrowing costlier, slowing spending and inflation. Lowering rates encourages borrowing and growth.
Bank deposits in the US are insured by the FDIC up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Credit unions are member-owned and have similar insurance through the NCUA.
units.try: Look at two local banks or credit unions (online or by visit). Compare a checking account at each: monthly fees, minimum balance, ATM access and overdraft fees. Decide which is better for a student and explain why.
check: What does the Fed usually do to slow high inflation?
Up to how much does FDIC insurance usually cover per depositor, per bank, per category?

learn: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxation, set by Congress and the President. During recessions, governments may cut taxes or raise spending; when spending exceeds revenue, there is a deficit, and accumulated deficits form the national debt.

The US federal income tax is progressive: higher slices of income are taxed at higher rates. Other taxes include payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare (FICA), sales taxes and property taxes, which often fund local schools.

Countries trade because of comparative advantage: each specializes in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost. Trade can raise total output, but some workers and industries lose out and may need support.

Trade barriers include tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas and embargoes. An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. A stronger dollar makes imports cheaper for Americans and US exports pricier abroad.
units.try: Look at the labels on ten items in your home, such as clothes and electronics. List where each was made. Pick one and write two reasons why it might be produced in that country, using the idea of comparative advantage.
check: What does a progressive income tax mean?
Higher income slices are taxed at higher rates
Everyone pays the same dollar amount

learn: Gross pay is what you earn before deductions. Net pay, or take-home pay, is what is left after federal and state income taxes, FICA (7.65% for most employees) and other deductions such as health insurance. Your W-4 form tells your employer how much to withhold.
Income depends on education, skills and the demand for your work. On average, workers with more education earn more over their careers, though apprenticeships and trades also offer strong pay.

A budget plans spending before it happens. One simple guideline is 50/30/20: about 50% of take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings and debt repayment. Track spending for a month to see where money really goes.
Build an emergency fund, often three to six months of essential expenses, to handle surprises like car repairs or job loss without going into debt.
units.try: Build a monthly budget for a first job paying $2,400 take-home. Using 50/30/20, needs get $1,200 (rent share, food, transport, phone), wants $720 and savings $480. List each item with a dollar amount and adjust until the total equals $2,400.

learn: Saving keeps money safe and accessible, as in a savings account. Investing buys assets that may grow over time, such as stocks and bonds, but with risk of loss. Generally, higher potential return comes with higher risk.

Compound interest earns interest on past interest. $1,000 at 7% per year grows to about $1,967 in 10 years and $7,612 in 30 years. The rule of 72 estimates doubling time: 72 ÷ interest rate. At 6%, money doubles in about 12 years.

A stock is a share of ownership in a company; a bond is a loan to a company or government. A mutual fund or index fund pools many investors’ money to buy a diversified mix. Diversification, spreading money across many investments, reduces risk.

Retirement accounts like a 401(k) or IRA have tax advantages. Many employers match part of 401(k) contributions, which is effectively extra pay. Starting early matters more than starting big because of compounding.
units.try: Compare two savers. Alex invests $100 a month from age 22 to 32, then stops. Sam invests $100 a month from 32 to 62. Look up a compound interest calculator or work with an assumed 7% return. Notice that Alex, who invested for only 10 years, can end up with a similar or larger balance because of early compounding.
check: Using the rule of 72, about how long to double at 8%?

learn: Credit lets you buy now and pay later, with interest. The annual percentage rate (APR) shows the yearly cost of borrowing. Credit cards often charge APRs above 20%, so carrying a balance is expensive.
Paying only the minimum can keep you in debt for years. A $2,000 balance at 22% APR, with $50 monthly payments, takes over five years to pay off and costs more than $1,400 in interest.

A credit score, usually from 300 to 850, summarizes how reliably you repay. The biggest factors are payment history and amounts owed (credit utilization). Paying on time and keeping balances below about 30% of limits helps.

Major loans include auto loans, mortgages and student loans. Federal student loans usually have lower fixed rates and flexible repayment compared with private loans. Before borrowing, compare total cost, not just the monthly payment.
units.try: Read the summary box from a sample credit card offer (many banks post them). Find the purchase APR, annual fee, late fee and grace period. Write a one-paragraph explanation of how you would use this card without paying any interest.
check: What is the biggest factor in most credit scores?

units.t: Consumer Protection, Insurance and Big Decisions
learn: Insurance pools risk: many people pay premiums so the few who suffer a loss are covered. Key terms include the deductible (what you pay first), the premium (the regular cost) and the coverage limit. Common types are health, auto, renters and life insurance.

Protect yourself from fraud and identity theft. Never share passwords or one-time codes, be suspicious of urgent requests for money or gift cards, and check your accounts regularly. You can get free credit reports and can freeze your credit with the three major bureaus.

When renting, read the lease carefully: rent, deposit, length, who pays utilities and rules for ending early. When buying a car, compare the total price, interest and insurance costs, not just the monthly payment.

Paying for college involves the FAFSA, which determines eligibility for federal grants, work-study and loans. Grants and scholarships do not need to be repaid. Compare net price, the cost after grants, when choosing schools.
units.try: You receive a text saying your bank account is locked and asking you to click a link and enter your password. Write the steps you should take instead, such as not clicking, contacting the bank using the number on your card or official app, and reporting the message.
check: The amount you pay before insurance pays
Which form determines eligibility for federal student aid?

rooms.about: An advanced course focused on fluent conversation, debate and presentation in Spanish, polishing advanced grammar while exploring the cultures, literature, music and current issues of the Spanish-speaking world.

units.t: Conversación: estrategias para hablar con fluidez
learn: Fluent speakers keep conversations moving with conectores. Useful ones: además (besides), sin embargo (however), por lo tanto (therefore), es decir (that is), en cambio (on the other hand) and a fin de cuentas (in the end).

To hold the floor while you think, use muletillas naturally: pues, bueno, o sea, a ver, este (common in Mexico). To ask for clarification: ¿Cómo dices?, ¿Me lo puedes repetir?, ¿Qué quieres decir con eso?

Show active listening: ¡No me digas! (no way!), ¡Qué va! (not at all!), Tienes toda la razón, Entiendo lo que dices, pero… Agreeing and disagreeing politely is key: Estoy de acuerdo contigo / No estoy del todo de acuerdo.

Register matters. Use tú with friends and family, and usted with elders, strangers and in formal settings. In much of Latin America, ustedes is the plural for both; in most of Spain, vosotros is the informal plural.
units.try: Record yourself talking for two minutes in Spanish about your plans after graduation. Use at least five conectores and two muletillas. Listen back and note any long English pauses. Try again and aim to replace each pause with a Spanish filler or connector.
check: Which pronoun would you use with a new school principal?

units.t: El subjuntivo en todas sus formas
learn: The present subjunctive expresses wishes, doubt, emotion and influence: Espero que vengas. Dudo que llueva. Form it from the yo form, drop -o, and add opposite endings: hablar → hable; comer → coma; tener → tenga.
The imperfect subjunctive is used in the past: Quería que vinieras. Form it from the ellos preterite, drop -ron, and add -ra endings: hablaron → hablara; tuvieron → tuviera; fueron → fuera.

Use the subjunctive after certain conjunctions: para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que, con tal de que. Also after cuando when the action is future: Cuando llegues, llámame. But use the indicative for habits: Cuando llego, como.

Si clauses: for unlikely or contrary-to-fact situations use imperfect subjunctive + conditional. Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría a Chile. For the past, use the pluperfect subjunctive: Si hubiera estudiado, habría aprobado.
units.try: Complete these sentences in Spanish: 1) Mis padres quieren que yo… 2) Si ganara la lotería, … 3) Antes de que termine el año, … 4) Si hubiera nacido en otro país, … Check that you used present subjunctive, conditional, present subjunctive and conditional perfect.
check: Si tuviera dinero, compraría un coche.
Si tengo dinero, compraría un coche.
Si tendría dinero, compro un coche.
What is the imperfect subjunctive of “ir” for yo?

learn: In a formal debate, structure your argument: tesis (claim), argumentos (reasons), pruebas (evidence) and conclusión. Introduce points with En primer lugar, En segundo lugar, Por último.

Persuasive phrases: Es evidente que (indicative follows), Es importante que (subjunctive follows), No cabe duda de que, Cabe destacar que. Remember: certainty takes the indicative; opinion and value judgments with es + adjective + que take the subjunctive.

To refute: Entiendo tu punto de vista, pero… / Eso no es del todo cierto porque… / Por el contrario… To concede: Es verdad que…, aunque… Aunque takes the subjunctive when the point is hypothetical or not accepted as fact.

Common debate themes in Spanish classes include el uso de la tecnología, el medio ambiente, la inmigración and la educación universitaria gratuita. Present both sides fairly and support claims with data.
units.try: Choose a debate topic, for example “Los estudiantes deberían usar uniformes.” Write a one-minute argument a favor and a one-minute argument en contra, each with three reasons and a conclusion. Practice delivering both sides aloud.
check: Which phrase must be followed by the subjunctive?
What does “Por último” mean in a debate?

learn: Spain’s history includes Iberians, Celts, Romans, Visigoths and nearly 800 years of Muslim rule in Al-Ándalus (711–1492). The Alhambra in Granada and the Mezquita of Córdoba are famous Moorish monuments. Spanish gained many Arabic words, like almohada, aceite and ojalá.

In 1492, Granada fell to the Catholic Monarchs, Jews were expelled, and Columbus reached the Americas. Spain built a vast empire, but its colonization brought violence, forced labor and devastating disease to Indigenous peoples.
The Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) led to the dictatorship of Francisco Franco until his death in 1975. Spain then became a democracy with a constitutional monarchy under the 1978 Constitution.

Spain has four widely spoken languages: castellano (Spanish), catalán, gallego and euskera (Basque, unrelated to any other known language). Regional identity is strong, and the country is divided into 17 comunidades autónomas.
units.try: Prepare a three-minute presentation in Spanish on one Spanish region, such as Andalucía, Cataluña, Galicia or el País Vasco. Include its language, one famous food, one festival and one historical fact. Use at least three past-tense verbs.
check: Which language spoken in Spain is unrelated to Spanish?
About how long was Muslim rule in parts of Spain?

learn: Latin America has deep Indigenous roots. The Maya built cities and a writing system; the Aztecs (Mexica) founded Tenochtitlan, now Mexico City; the Inca ran an empire along the Andes. Today millions speak Indigenous languages such as quechua, guaraní, náhuatl and maya.

Most of Latin America won independence from Spain between 1810 and 1825, led by figures such as Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín and Miguel Hidalgo. The region’s culture blends Indigenous, European and African heritage.
Spanish varies by region. In Argentina and Uruguay, people use voseo: vos sos instead of tú eres. Words differ too: a bus is camión in Mexico, guagua in the Caribbean and colectivo in Argentina.
In Paraguay, guaraní is an official language alongside Spanish, and most people speak it. In Peru and Bolivia, quechua and aymara are also official.
units.try: Find a short video or podcast clip of speakers from three countries, such as Mexico, Argentina and Spain. Listen for one difference in pronunciation, one in vocabulary and one in grammar (like voseo or vosotros). Write your findings in Spanish.
check: In which country is guaraní an official language?

learn: Spanish-language literature is rich. Miguel de Cervantes’s Don Quijote (1605, 1615) is often called the first modern novel. Its idealistic knight and practical squire, Sancho Panza, explore the line between fantasy and reality.
Gabriel García Márquez of Colombia won the 1982 Nobel Prize. His novel Cien años de soledad is a landmark of realismo mágico, where magical events are told as if they were ordinary.

Poets include Pablo Neruda (Chile, Nobel 1971), known for love poems and odes to everyday objects; Gabriela Mistral (Chile), the first Latin American Nobel winner in literature in 1945; and Federico García Lorca of Spain.

Jorge Luis Borges of Argentina wrote short stories full of labyrinths, mirrors and infinite libraries. When reading, identify el narrador, el tema, el tono and los símbolos, and discuss them in Spanish.
units.try: Write your own oda to an everyday object in Spanish, in the spirit of Neruda’s odes, such as “Oda a mi mochila.” Write 12 short lines describing the object with vivid adjectives and comparisons using como.
check: Magical events told as if they were ordinary

learn: Famous Spanish painters include Diego Velázquez (Las Meninas), Francisco de Goya and Pablo Picasso, whose Guernica (1937) protests the bombing of a Basque town during the Civil War.

Mexican muralists Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros painted public walls with scenes of history and workers. Frida Kahlo painted intense self-portraits mixing personal pain with Mexican identity.

Music styles include flamenco (Spain), tango (Argentina), salsa (with Cuban roots, developed in New York), cumbia (Colombia), mariachi (Mexico), merengue and bachata (Dominican Republic) and reggaetón (Puerto Rico and Panama).

To describe art in Spanish: En primer plano (in the foreground), al fondo (in the background), los colores son cálidos/fríos, el artista quiere expresar…, me llama la atención… (catches my attention).
units.try: Look at an image of Picasso’s Guernica. Write a description in Spanish of at least eight sentences: what is in the foreground and background, the colors, the emotions and what you think the artist wanted to say about war.
check: Which painting protests the bombing of a Basque town?
Which music style is most associated with Argentina?

units.t: Temas actuales: sociedad y medio ambiente
learn: Key vocabulary for current issues: el cambio climático, la deforestación, la sequía (drought), la desigualdad (inequality), la migración, los derechos humanos, la energía renovable, el desarrollo sostenible.

The Amazon rainforest spans nine countries, including Brasil, Perú, Colombia and Bolivia. Deforestation threatens biodiversity and Indigenous communities. Glaciers in the Andes supply water to cities like La Paz and Lima and are shrinking.

To discuss solutions use: Habría que… (we should), Sería mejor que + imperfect subjunctive, Es necesario que + present subjunctive, Propongo que… Example: Es necesario que reduzcamos el uso de plástico.
To report what others said, use indirect speech: Él dijo: “Voy a reciclar.” becomes Él dijo que iba a reciclar. Verb tenses usually shift back into the past.
units.try: Read a short Spanish news article (from a Spanish-language newspaper site) about an environmental or social issue. Write a 150-word summary in Spanish using indirect speech at least twice and propose one solution using Es necesario que.
check: Which correctly completes: Es necesario que nosotros ___ más agua.

learn: Spanish is spoken by over 500 million people as a first language and is the second most spoken native language in the world. In the US, over 40 million people speak Spanish at home, so bilingual skills are valued in health care, law, education and business.

A formal letter or email opens with Estimado/a señor/a + last name: and closes with Atentamente or Saludos cordiales. Use usted forms throughout and polite conditionals: ¿Podría enviarme…? Me gustaría solicitar…

Job interview phrases: Tengo experiencia en…, Mis puntos fuertes son…, Trabajo bien en equipo, Hablo inglés y español con fluidez. Common questions: ¿Por qué quiere trabajar aquí? ¿Cuáles son sus metas profesionales?

Interpreters work with spoken language; translators work with written text. Good translation conveys meaning, not word-for-word matches. Watch for false friends: embarazada means pregnant, not embarrassed; actual means current.
units.try: Write a formal email in Spanish applying for a summer job as a camp counselor. Include a greeting, your experience, why you want the job, your availability and a polite closing. Use usted forms and at least two conditional verbs.
check: Which is a formal email closing?

learn: A strong oral presentation in Spanish has an introduction (Hoy voy a hablar de…), a body with clear sections, and a conclusion (Para concluir…, En resumen…). Speak to your audience and use notes with key words, not full sentences.
Review the main tenses: present, preterite (completed actions), imperfect (descriptions and habits in the past), future, conditional, perfect tenses with haber, and the subjunctive moods.

Preterite vs imperfect: Cuando era niño, vivía en Texas (background, imperfect). Un día conocí a mi mejor amigo (specific event, preterite). Imperfect sets the scene; preterite moves the story forward.

Keep improving after this course: watch films and series in Spanish with Spanish subtitles, read news, listen to music, talk with native speakers, and consider the AP or IB exam or college placement tests.
units.try: Give a five-minute final presentation in Spanish about a Spanish-speaking country you would like to visit. Include its history, culture, a current issue and why you want to go. Use at least four different tenses, including one si clause.
check: Which tense describes background in the past?

rooms.about: An advanced studio year in which students develop a sustained personal investigation, build a cohesive portfolio, write about their work and prepare to exhibit and apply to art programs.

learn: An artistic voice is the recognizable combination of subject, style, materials and ideas that makes work yours. It grows from what you care about and from making lots of work, not from waiting for inspiration.
Start by reviewing your past work. Sort pieces into strongest and weakest, then look for patterns: recurring subjects, colors, marks or themes. These patterns are clues to your interests.
Keep a sketchbook as a visual journal. Fill it with quick studies, collected images, notes, color tests and ideas. Many artists set a goal such as one page per day; quantity leads to quality.
Study artists you admire, but analyze rather than copy: ask why a composition works, how a color palette creates mood or what technique made a texture. Then apply the principle in your own way.
units.try: Lay out ten pieces of your past art. Write three words that describe each. Circle words that appear more than once. Use those repeated words to write a one-sentence statement beginning “My work explores…”
check: What best builds an artistic voice?
Making a lot of work and noticing your patterns
How should you use the work of artists you admire?
Analyze why it works and apply the ideas your own way
Trace it and sign your name
Avoid looking at any other art

learn: A sustained investigation is a body of work, often 12 to 15 pieces, that explores one guiding question through practice, experimentation and revision. Example: “How can everyday objects represent memories of family?”

A good inquiry question is open-ended and personal. It should allow many answers and approaches. Avoid questions that are only a subject, like “cats,” and frame them as explorations, like “How can animals reflect human moods?”
Show growth over time. Include experiments, failures that taught you something and changes in direction. Process work, such as sketches and test pieces, can be documented alongside finished works.
Plan the investigation with a timeline. Set milestones for idea development, materials testing, main works and reflection. Check in every two weeks to evaluate what is working.
units.try: Write three possible inquiry questions for a year-long investigation. For each, sketch three thumbnail ideas showing different ways to explore it. Choose the question that excites you most and generates the most varied ideas.
check: A body of work exploring one guiding question
Which is the strongest inquiry question?
How can light reveal hidden emotions in portraits?

learn: Drawing is the foundation of most visual art. Advanced skills include accurate proportion through sighting (measuring with a pencil at arm’s length), using negative space and building form with value from highlight to core shadow to cast shadow.

Mark-making is how lines and textures carry expression. Hatching, cross-hatching, stippling, scribbling and blending each create a different feel. Varying pressure and speed changes line weight and energy.

Try unconventional tools: charcoal on toned paper with white highlights, ink with a stick or brush, or erasing into a charcoal-covered surface to pull out light. Material choice is part of the meaning.
Gesture drawings of 30 seconds to 2 minutes capture movement. Sustained drawings of several hours build detail. Practicing both improves accuracy and expressiveness.
units.try: Set a still life of three objects under one lamp. Do five 1-minute gesture drawings, then one 45-minute value drawing in charcoal. Make a value scale of seven steps first and match at least five values in your drawing.
check: Measuring proportions with a pencil at arm’s length
What do gesture drawings mainly capture?

learn: Color theory guides choices. Complementary colors sit opposite on the color wheel and intensify each other. Analogous colors sit side by side and create harmony. Warm colors tend to advance; cool colors tend to recede.

Value matters more than hue for readability. Take a black-and-white photo of a painting to check if its contrast works. A limited palette, such as three primaries plus white, helps build color-mixing skill and unity.
Mixed media combines materials, such as acrylic with collage, ink, fabric or found objects. Use a sturdy surface like heavy paper, board or canvas, and plan layers from flat to thick.
Work safely: ventilate the room, read labels, avoid eating while painting, never pour solvents down the drain, and wash hands after handling pigments.
units.try: Paint the same simple subject three times on small boards: once in complementary colors, once in analogous colors and once in grayscale. Compare the moods and write two sentences about how color changed the meaning.
check: Colors opposite each other on the color wheel
Colors next to each other on the wheel
Why photograph a painting in black and white?

learn: Sculpture can be additive (building up, as in clay modeling or assemblage) or subtractive (carving away, as in stone or wood carving). Other methods include casting and constructing with wire, cardboard or wood.
Think in the round: a sculpture must work from every angle. Consider mass, volume, balance, texture and the space around the object. Turn your piece regularly as you work.

Installation art transforms a whole space so viewers walk into the work. Light, sound and arrangement become part of the art. Many installations are temporary and are documented with photos and video.
Use tools safely: cut away from your body, use the right glue for each material, wear gloves and eye protection when needed, and ask for supervision with hot glue guns, saws or kilns.
units.try: Build a small cardboard sculpture (no larger than 30 cm) representing an emotion. Use only cardboard, scissors and glue. Make it interesting from four sides. Photograph it from four angles and choose the strongest view.
check: Carving wood is which kind of sculpture method?
Art that transforms a whole space viewers enter
A small drawing in a frame

learn: Photography uses light, composition and timing. The rule of thirds places key subjects along imaginary lines dividing the frame into thirds. Leading lines guide the eye, and framing uses doorways or branches to surround a subject.
Exposure depends on aperture (how wide the lens opens), shutter speed (how long it stays open) and ISO (sensor sensitivity). A fast shutter freezes motion; a slow one creates blur.
Digital tools allow editing, layering and illustration. Work non-destructively using layers and keep your original file. Save in high resolution, at least 300 pixels per inch for print.
Respect copyright: use your own photos or images you have permission to use. Ask permission before photographing people for public display, especially minors.
units.try: Take 30 photos around your home on one theme, such as “shadows.” Use the rule of thirds, leading lines and framing in at least five each. Choose your best three and edit only brightness, contrast and cropping.
check: What does a fast shutter speed do?
What resolution is usually recommended for print?

learn: Critique is structured discussion of artwork to help it improve. A common method is Describe (what do you see?), Analyze (how are elements and principles used?), Interpret (what does it mean?) and Judge (how successful is it, and why?).
Give specific, kind and useful feedback. Instead of “I like it,” say “The warm red in the corner pulls my eye away from the face; could you cool it down?”
Receive feedback openly. Take notes, ask clarifying questions and avoid defending yourself in the moment. Later decide which suggestions fit your intent.
Revision is normal for professional artists. Sometimes a piece needs small changes; sometimes the lesson is best applied to the next work.
units.try: Hold a mini critique with a family member or friend. Show one artwork and ask them three questions: What do you notice first? What do you think it is about? What is one thing that confuses you? Write their answers and one change you will make.
check: What is the first step of the four-step critique method?
Which is the most useful feedback?
The bright red corner pulls attention away from the face

units.t: Writing About Art: The Artist Statement
learn: An artist statement explains what you make, how and why. It is usually 100 to 300 words, written in first person and plain language. It should help viewers connect to the work, not replace it.
A clear structure: 1) what your work is about (theme or question), 2) materials and process, and 3) what you hope viewers experience. Avoid vague words like “unique” or heavy jargon.
Applications and exhibits often ask for short descriptions of individual works, including title, medium, size and year, for example: Untitled Memory, charcoal on paper, 18 × 24 in., 2026.
Read your statement aloud. If it sounds like something any artist could write, add specific details about your subjects, materials or experiences.
units.try: Write a 150-word artist statement for your sustained investigation using the three-part structure. Then cut it to 50 words. Notice which details you kept; those are the heart of your work.
check: About how long is a typical artist statement?
Which detail belongs in an artwork label?
The price of your art supplies

learn: A portfolio is a curated selection of your best work, often 10 to 20 pieces. Quality and variety of skill matter more than quantity. Include strong observational drawing plus work that shows your ideas and voice.
Order matters: start and end with your strongest pieces. Group related works so the portfolio tells a coherent story of your interests and growth.

Document 2D work in even, indirect light, square to the camera, with no glare or background showing. Photograph 3D work against a plain backdrop from several angles. Name files clearly, such as Lastname_Title_Year.
Many colleges and Advanced Placement art exams require digital submissions. Check each program’s requirements for number of works, file size and written descriptions well before deadlines.
units.try: Photograph five of your best works using a window as soft daylight and a plain wall or sheet as background. Crop each image so only the art shows. Arrange them in an order that tells a story and write one sentence explaining your order.
check: What matters most in a portfolio?
Having as many pieces as possible
In even, indirect light, square to the camera
With a flash pointed directly at it
At a steep angle in a dark room

units.t: Exhibition and Life After High School
learn: Exhibiting means planning a show: selecting works, arranging them for flow, hanging at a consistent height (center around 57 to 60 inches from the floor is common), labeling and promoting the event.
Art careers include fine artist, illustrator, graphic designer, animator, photographer, architect, art teacher, art therapist, museum curator and game artist. Many combine several roles.
Paths include art schools, university art programs, community colleges and self-directed study. Portfolio days and reviews let students get feedback from many schools at once.
Keep making art after graduation. Join community studios, take workshops, share work responsibly online and stay curious. A lifelong creative practice benefits well-being whatever your career.
units.try: Plan a home exhibit of 6 to 8 works on a wall or table. Arrange them so the center of each piece sits about 57 inches from the floor, write labels, and invite family or friends for a 15-minute walk-through where you talk about one piece.
check: About what height is commonly used for the center of hung artwork?

rooms.about: An advanced year of ensemble performance and musicianship: tone, intonation, rhythm, sight-reading, ear training, conducting, rehearsal skills and leadership, ending in a capstone performance.

learn: An ensemble is any group that performs together: choir, band, orchestra, jazz combo or chamber group. Success depends less on individual flash and more on listening, blending and shared timing.
Good ensemble habits: arrive early, warm up, mark your music in pencil, watch the conductor, and listen across the group. Professional players often say they listen more than they play.
Each part has a role. Melody carries the main tune, harmony supports it, the bass line gives the foundation and the rhythm section keeps time. Know when your part leads and when it accompanies.

Daily individual practice makes rehearsals productive. Practice slowly with a metronome, isolate hard passages, and record yourself. Short focused sessions of 20 to 30 minutes beat long distracted ones.
units.try: Record yourself singing or playing a familiar 16-bar passage with a recording or metronome. Listen back and rate yourself 1 to 5 on rhythm, pitch and tone. Choose the weakest and practice it slowly for 10 minutes, then record again.
check: What is the most important ensemble skill?
What should you use to mark your music?

learn: Tone is the quality of your sound. A good tone is centered, resonant and controlled. For singers and wind players, it depends on breath support: inhaling low and deep, expanding the lower ribs and abdomen, and using steady airflow.
Posture affects tone. Stand or sit tall with relaxed shoulders, feet flat and head level. Tension in the jaw, neck or shoulders restricts airflow and tone.
String players produce tone with bow weight, speed and contact point. Closer to the bridge gives a brighter, louder sound; closer to the fingerboard gives a softer, warmer sound.
Long tones, holding a single note for 8 to 16 counts at steady volume, are a classic exercise to build control. Crescendo and decrescendo on long tones builds dynamic control.
units.try: Practice breathing: inhale for 4 counts through the mouth, feeling your lower ribs expand, then exhale on a hiss for 8, then 12, then 16 counts. Then sing or play a long tone for 8 counts, getting louder for 4 and softer for 4.
check: Where should a deep breath expand?

learn: Intonation is playing or singing in tune. When two pitches are slightly out of tune, you hear beats, a wobbling in the sound. As the pitches match, the beats slow down and disappear.
Concert A is usually tuned to 440 Hz. Wind players adjust slides or barrels; string players adjust pegs and fine tuners; singers adjust by listening and matching.

Tuning is not fixed. Major thirds in chords often need to be slightly lower than an electronic tuner shows, and the fifths slightly wider, to sound pure. This is why ensembles listen rather than only watching tuners.
