Cold instruments play flat and warm ones play sharp. Tune after warming up, and keep checking during rehearsal.
units.try: With a partner, a recording or a tuner app’s drone, sustain a single pitch together. Slowly move your pitch slightly up and down and listen for the beats to speed up or slow down. Find the point where they vanish.
check: A wobble heard when two pitches are slightly out of tune
What frequency is concert A usually tuned to?

learn: Meter is the organization of beats. In 4/4, there are four quarter-note beats per measure. In 3/4, three. In 6/8, six eighth notes grouped in two big beats, giving a lilting feel.
Subdivision means feeling smaller units inside the beat. Counting “1-e-and-a” for sixteenth notes helps you play precisely. Ensembles that subdivide together stay together.
Syncopation places accents on weak beats or offbeats, common in jazz, funk and Latin music. Swing rhythm plays pairs of eighth notes long-short, roughly like a triplet.
Odd meters such as 5/4 and 7/8 group beats unevenly, like 3+2 or 2+2+3. Tempo terms include largo (very slow), andante (walking pace), allegro (fast) and presto (very fast).
units.try: Set a metronome to 80 beats per minute. Clap quarter notes for one measure, eighth notes, triplets, then sixteenths, saying the counts aloud. Then clap a 7/8 pattern grouped 2+2+3, accenting the first note of each group.
check: Two big beats, each divided into three

learn: Sight-reading is performing music you have never seen before. It is tested at auditions and used in professional work. It improves with daily practice on easy music.

Before you start, scan the piece for 30 to 60 seconds. Check the key signature, time signature, tempo, dynamics, repeats, and any tricky rhythms or accidentals. Many teachers use the acronym STARS: signatures, tempo, accidentals, rhythm, signs.
While reading, keep a steady pulse and do not stop to fix mistakes. Look ahead a measure or two. A missed note is better than a broken rhythm.
Singers use solfège (do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti) or numbers to hear pitches before singing. Instrumentalists can finger or silently sing passages while scanning.
units.try: Find a simple piece of music you have never played or sung, such as a hymn or folk song. Give yourself 60 seconds to scan using STARS, then perform it once without stopping. Repeat with a new piece every day for a week.
check: When sight-reading, what is most important to keep?
What should you check before sight-reading?
Key, time signature, tempo and tricky spots

learn: Ear training builds the ability to recognize intervals, chords and patterns by sound. Intervals can be learned with reference songs: a perfect fourth starts many marches and anthems; a perfect fifth sounds open and hollow.
Triads are three-note chords. Major sounds bright (root, major third, perfect fifth); minor sounds darker (root, minor third, perfect fifth); diminished sounds tense; augmented sounds unresolved.
Many songs use chord progressions based on scale degrees. In C major, I = C, IV = F, V = G and vi = A minor. The I–IV–V–I and I–V–vi–IV progressions appear in countless songs.
A cadence ends a phrase. An authentic cadence (V–I) sounds final; a half cadence ends on V and sounds unfinished; a deceptive cadence (V–vi) surprises the ear.
units.try: At a keyboard or with a free piano app, play C–E–G (major) then C–E♭–G (minor). Have someone play one at random and name it by ear 10 times. Then play I–IV–V–I in C major (C, F, G, C chords) and sing the bass notes.
check: Which notes form a C major triad?

learn: Conductors show tempo, dynamics, entrances and character with gestures. Basic patterns: 2/4 is down-up; 3/4 is down-right-up; 4/4 is down-left-right-up. The first beat, the downbeat, is always down.
The preparatory beat, one beat before the music starts, shows tempo and style. A cutoff is a small loop or closing gesture that ends a sound together.

A full score shows all parts stacked. Woodwinds are usually on top, then brass, percussion and strings at the bottom. Some instruments are transposing: a B♭ clarinet sounds a whole step lower than written.
The conductor’s left hand often shows dynamics, cues and expression while the right keeps time. Eye contact and breathing with the ensemble make entrances clear.
units.try: Put on a recording of a piece in 4/4 and conduct the pattern (down-left-right-up) for one minute. Then try a waltz in 3/4. Add a preparatory beat and a clear cutoff, and practice in a mirror.
check: Where are strings usually placed in a full orchestral score?

learn: Musical style changes across eras. Baroque music (1600–1750) features steady rhythm and ornaments; Classical (1750–1820) favors balance and clarity; Romantic (1820–1900) emphasizes emotion and flexible tempo (rubato); 20th-century music explores new sounds and forms.
Articulation shapes notes: staccato (short and detached), legato (smooth and connected), accent (emphasized) and tenuto (held full value). Matching articulation across a section creates unity.
Dynamics range from pianissimo (pp, very soft) to fortissimo (ff, very loud). Phrasing means shaping a musical sentence, often growing toward a high point and relaxing at the end.
Jazz and popular styles have their own conventions, such as swing feel, blue notes and improvisation. Listening to great recordings is the best way to learn a style.
units.try: Choose one simple melody and perform it four ways: all staccato, all legato, with a crescendo to the highest note, and with rubato. Record each and decide which interpretation best fits the melody’s character.

learn: Chamber music is performed by small groups, usually one player per part, without a conductor. Examples include a string quartet, brass quintet or vocal quartet. Players lead with breaths, nods and eye contact.

Effective rehearsals have a plan: warm-up, focused work on the hardest sections, run-throughs and goals for next time. Fix problems by isolating a few measures, slowing down, then building back to tempo.
Section leaders help others by modeling good tone and preparation, communicating kindly and making decisions about bowings or breaths.
Feedback in groups should be specific and respectful: “Can we try measure 12 softer so the melody comes through?” rather than “You’re too loud.”
units.try: Form a small group with friends or family (singing works too). Choose a round like a simple folk song. Plan a 20-minute rehearsal with warm-up, two problem spots and a final run. Start the group without a conductor by giving a clear breath cue.
check: What usually leads a chamber ensemble?
The players, using breaths, nods and eye contact
What is the best way to fix a hard passage in rehearsal?
Isolate it, slow down, then build back to tempo
Play the whole piece repeatedly at full speed

learn: Performance anxiety is normal; even professionals feel nerves. Helpful strategies include thorough preparation, slow breathing (inhale for 4, exhale for 6), positive self-talk and practicing performances in front of others.
Stage presence includes walking on confidently, acknowledging applause with a bow, staying focused during rests, and recovering from mistakes without showing them.
A capstone performance demonstrates your growth. Choose repertoire that shows a range of styles and skills, but is within your reach so you can perform it musically.

Music continues after high school through college ensembles, community bands and choirs, church or civic groups, teaching lessons, music careers or playing for joy. Studies link group music-making to well-being.
units.try: Hold a practice concert at home. Choose two contrasting pieces, introduce each in one or two sentences to your audience, perform them, and bow. Afterward write three things that went well and one goal for next time.
check: Which is a helpful strategy for performance nerves?
Avoiding practice in front of anyone
What should you do after a mistake on stage?

rooms.about: Preparing for independent adult life: designing your own fitness and nutrition plan, caring for mental health and sleep, understanding substance-use risks, healthy relationships and consent, and basic first aid and emergency response.

learn: Adults are advised to get at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week (or 75 minutes vigorous), plus muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days. Teens are advised to get 60 minutes of activity daily.
The FITT principle designs a plan: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long) and Type (what activity). Progress gradually, increasing volume by about 10% a week to avoid injury.
The five health-related fitness components are cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. A balanced plan addresses all five.
Choose activities you enjoy, since consistency matters most. Options after high school include running, cycling, swimming, recreational leagues, hiking, dance, yoga and gym classes.
units.try: Write a four-week FITT plan for yourself with three cardio sessions and two strength sessions per week. Include warm-ups and cool-downs. Track each session in a log and increase one variable slightly each week.
check: How much moderate aerobic activity is recommended for adults each week?
What does the “I” in FITT stand for?

learn: Strength training builds muscle, bone density and metabolism. Beginners can do 2–3 sets of 8–12 repetitions for major muscle groups with weight that feels challenging by the last reps but allows good form.
Key movement patterns: squat, hinge (like a deadlift), push (push-up), pull (row) and carry. Bodyweight versions are a safe place to start.

Safe technique: keep a neutral spine, brace your core, control the movement in both directions, breathe out during the effort and never sacrifice form for heavier weight. Use a spotter for heavy bench presses.
Rest 48 hours between hard sessions for the same muscle group. Muscles grow during recovery, which needs sleep and enough protein, roughly 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight daily for most adults.
units.try: Do a bodyweight circuit: 10 squats, 8 push-ups (on knees or a wall if needed), 10 glute bridges, 10 rows using a sturdy table edge or resistance band, and a 30-second plank. Rest 1 minute and repeat twice. Focus on slow, controlled form.
check: When should you exhale during a lift?
How long should a muscle group usually rest between hard sessions?

learn: A balanced plate is about half fruits and vegetables, a quarter whole grains and a quarter lean protein, with a dairy or calcium-rich option. Drink water as your main beverage.

Read nutrition labels: check serving size first, then calories, saturated fat, sodium (aim under 2,300 mg a day) and added sugars (under 10% of daily calories). The % Daily Value shows how much a serving contributes; 5% or less is low, 20% or more is high.

Cooking at home saves money and gives control over ingredients. Budget staples include beans, eggs, oats, rice, frozen vegetables, seasonal fruit and canned fish. Plan meals weekly and shop with a list.
Food safety: wash hands, keep raw meat separate, cook poultry to 165°F, refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and keep the fridge at 40°F or below.
units.try: Plan three days of meals on a budget of $10 per day. Use at least three budget staples, include a vegetable at every meal, and write a shopping list with estimated prices. Cook one of the meals.
check: To what temperature should poultry be cooked?
On a nutrition label, what %DV is considered high?

learn: Teens need 8–10 hours of sleep and adults 7 or more. Poor sleep affects mood, memory, immune function and driving safety. Keep a regular schedule, limit screens an hour before bed, and avoid caffeine late in the day.

Stress is a normal response to challenges. Short-term stress can motivate, but chronic stress harms health. Coping skills include exercise, time management, talking with others, deep breathing and breaking tasks into steps.

Mental health conditions such as anxiety and depression are common and treatable. Warning signs include lasting sadness, withdrawal from friends, changes in sleep or appetite and loss of interest. Getting help is a sign of strength.
Help is available from trusted adults, school counselors, doctors and therapists. In the US, you can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline any time. In an emergency, call 911.
units.try: For one week, log your bedtime, wake time, screen use before bed and mood each morning (1 to 5). At the end, look for patterns. Choose one change, like a fixed bedtime, and try it the next week.
check: How many hours of sleep do teens need?
What number reaches the US Suicide & Crisis Lifeline?

learn: Alcohol is a depressant that slows the brain and reactions. It is illegal to buy under age 21 in the US. Drinking large amounts quickly can cause alcohol poisoning, a medical emergency. Never drive after drinking or ride with a driver who has.
Nicotine, found in cigarettes and vapes, is highly addictive, and teen brains are especially vulnerable. Vaping can expose users to nicotine and other harmful chemicals.

Misusing prescription drugs, such as taking someone else’s medicine, can be dangerous. Counterfeit pills may contain fentanyl, which can be deadly in tiny amounts. Naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose; call 911 too.

Refusal skills help: say no clearly, suggest another activity, use humor, or leave. Friends who respect you will accept your choice. Help for substance use is available through doctors and the national helpline at 1-800-662-4357.
units.try: Write and practice three short ways to refuse an offer of alcohol or vaping at a party, such as “No thanks, I’m driving,” “I’ve got a game tomorrow,” or simply “No, I’m good.” Role-play them out loud with a friend or family member.
check: What can reverse an opioid overdose?
What type of drug is alcohol?

learn: Healthy relationships, with friends, family or partners, are built on respect, trust, honesty, good communication and support for each other’s goals. Each person keeps their own friends, interests and identity.

Warning signs of an unhealthy relationship include controlling behavior, extreme jealousy, checking someone’s phone, insults, isolating someone from friends, threats or any violence. Abuse is never the victim’s fault.

Consent means a clear, freely given, enthusiastic yes to any physical contact. It can be withdrawn at any time, cannot be given under pressure, and cannot be given by someone who is asleep, intoxicated or underage. Silence is not consent.

Use “I” statements to communicate: “I feel hurt when plans change without telling me.” If you or a friend need help, talk to a trusted adult or counselor, or contact a dating abuse or domestic violence hotline.
units.try: Write two short scenarios: one showing a healthy disagreement between friends and one showing a controlling behavior. For each, list what makes it healthy or unhealthy and write an “I” statement someone could use.
check: Which is a sign of an unhealthy relationship?
Can consent be withdrawn after it is given?

learn: In any emergency, first check that the scene is safe, then check the person, call 911 (or have someone call), and care for them until help arrives. Use gloves if available.
For bleeding, apply firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth and do not remove it if it soaks through; add more on top. For severe limb bleeding that will not stop, a tourniquet may be needed.
For minor burns, cool under cool running water for at least 10 minutes; do not use ice or butter. Cover loosely with a clean, non-stick dressing. Seek care for large, deep or facial burns.
For a suspected sprain, use rest, ice wrapped in cloth (20 minutes at a time), compression and elevation. Do not move someone with a possible head, neck or back injury unless they are in danger.
units.try: Build or check a home first aid kit. It should include adhesive bandages, gauze, tape, gloves, antiseptic wipes, scissors, a cold pack, tweezers and an emergency contact list. Practice applying a pressure bandage to a family member’s arm.
check: What is the first step in any emergency?
Check that the scene is safe
How should you treat a minor burn?
Cool it under running water for at least 10 minutes

learn: If an adult collapses and is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 911 and send someone for an AED, then start chest compressions. Push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 2 inches deep, at 100–120 compressions per minute.

Hands-only CPR is recommended for untrained bystanders helping an adult who suddenly collapses. Trained rescuers give 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. Let the chest fully rise between compressions.
An AED (automated external defibrillator) analyzes heart rhythm and can deliver a shock. Turn it on and follow its voice prompts. It is designed to be used by anyone.

For choking, if the person cannot speak, cough or breathe, give abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich maneuver): stand behind them, place a fist above the navel and thrust inward and upward. For infants, use back blows and chest thrusts.
units.try: Practice compression rhythm on a firm pillow (never on a person). Set a metronome to 110 beats per minute and push straight down with locked arms for two minutes. Notice how tiring it is, which is why rescuers switch every two minutes.
check: What is the correct rate of chest compressions?

learn: Driving safety: always wear a seatbelt, never text or drink and drive, follow speed limits, and get enough sleep before long drives. Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death for US teens.

Prepare for disasters: make a family plan with a meeting place and out-of-area contact, and keep a kit with water (one gallon per person per day for at least three days), nonperishable food, a flashlight, batteries, medicines and copies of documents.
Online safety: use strong unique passwords, enable two-factor authentication, think before sharing personal information or images, and remember that posts can be permanent.
Personal safety: stay aware of your surroundings, share plans with someone you trust, trust your instincts, and know how to reach emergency services.
units.try: With your family, make an emergency plan. Choose a meeting place near home and one outside the neighborhood, list emergency contacts, and check whether you have three days of water and food. Write the plan on one page and post it.
check: How much water should a kit hold per person per day?

learn: As an adult, you manage your own health care. Schedule yearly checkups, dental cleanings about every six months and eye exams as advised. Keep a list of your medications, allergies and vaccinations.
Health insurance helps pay medical costs. Know key terms: premium, deductible, copay and in-network providers. In the US, young adults can usually stay on a parent’s plan until age 26.

Evaluate health information critically. Check who wrote it, whether it cites research, if it is selling something, and whether it agrees with reputable medical organizations. Be wary of miracle cures.

Wellness has many dimensions: physical, emotional, social, intellectual, environmental and financial. Small daily habits, such as moving, sleeping, eating well and connecting with people, add up over a lifetime.
units.try: Create a personal health record: list your doctor, dentist, allergies, medications, vaccination dates you can find and your insurance information. Then set three wellness goals for your first year after high school, one physical, one emotional and one social.
check: Until what age can young adults usually stay on a parent’s health plan in the US?
Which is a red flag in health information?

rooms.about: The big ideas of computing: how data is represented, how algorithms and programs work, how the internet connects the world, and how computing affects society, privacy and security.

learn: Programs are built through an iterative process: investigate the problem, design a solution, prototype, test and refine. Repeating this cycle catches problems early and improves the product.
Collaboration brings diverse perspectives that reduce bias and catch errors. Pair programming has a driver who types and a navigator who reviews, and they switch roles often.

Programs have inputs (data from users, sensors or files), outputs (text, sound, images or actions) and behavior: what the program does in response. Clear documentation and comments help others understand code.

Errors are normal. Syntax errors break language rules; logic errors produce wrong results; runtime errors happen while running, like dividing by zero. Debug by testing small parts, printing values and checking expected outputs.
units.try: Find the logic error: average = a + b / 2, intended to average two numbers. Step 1: test with a = 4, b = 6; the result is 4 + 3 = 7, not 5. Step 2: division happens before addition. Step 3: fix with parentheses: average = (a + b) / 2, which gives 5.
check: Which kind of error produces a wrong answer but no crash?
In pair programming, what does the navigator do?

learn: Computers store all data as bits, binary digits 0 and 1. Eight bits make a byte. With n bits you can represent 2ⁿ different values: 8 bits give 256 values (0 to 255).
Binary place values are powers of 2: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. So 1011 in binary is 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11 in decimal. Hexadecimal uses base 16 (0–9, A–F) as shorthand: FF = 255.

Text is stored with codes like ASCII and Unicode; capital A is 65. Images are grids of pixels, each with red, green and blue values from 0 to 255. Sound is sampled many times per second, often 44,100.
Fixed bit limits cause overflow errors when a number is too large, and round-off errors because some decimals, like 0.1, cannot be stored exactly in binary.
units.try: Convert 45 to binary. Step 1: largest power of 2 not above 45 is 32; 45 − 32 = 13. Step 2: 16 is too big, write 0. Step 3: 8 fits; 13 − 8 = 5. Step 4: 4 fits; 5 − 4 = 1. Step 5: 2 does not fit, write 0. Step 6: 1 fits. Result: 101101.
check: How many values can 8 bits represent?

learn: Compression reduces file size. Lossless compression, used in ZIP and PNG, lets you rebuild the original exactly. Lossy compression, used in JPEG and MP3, removes less noticeable details for much smaller files.
Run-length encoding is a simple lossless method: AAAABBBCC becomes 4A3B2C. It works well when data has long runs of repeated values.
Metadata is data about data, such as a photo’s date, location and camera settings. It helps organize and search files but may reveal private information.

Data analysis finds patterns. Steps include collecting, cleaning (fixing missing or inconsistent values), filtering, visualizing and interpreting. Large datasets can reveal trends but may contain bias, and correlation is not causation.
units.try: Compress WWWWWWBBBWWWWBB with run-length encoding. Count each run: 6 W, 3 B, 4 W, 2 B. Result: 6W3B4W2B, 8 characters instead of 15. Now try WBWBWB: it becomes 1W1B1W1B1W1B, which is longer, showing compression does not always help.
check: Which type of compression allows perfect reconstruction?
The largest file on a computer

learn: A variable is a named storage location for a value. In Python: score = 0 assigns 0 to score. Later, score = score + 10 updates it to 10. The right side is evaluated first.
Expressions combine values and operators: + − * / for arithmetic, and % (modulus) for remainder. 17 % 5 is 2. Modulus is useful to test even numbers: n % 2 == 0.
Boolean expressions are True or False. Comparison operators include ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=. Logical operators and, or and not combine conditions.
A list stores many values in order: names = [“Ana”, “Ben”, “Cy”]. In Python, indexes start at 0, so names[0] is Ana. Use append to add and len(names) to count items. Lists help manage complexity.
units.try: Trace this code: x = 5, then y = x * 2, then x = x + y, then print(x % 4). Step 1: y = 10. Step 2: x = 5 + 10 = 15. Step 3: 15 % 4 = 3, since 15 = 3 × 4 + 3. Output: 3.
check: In Python, what index does the first list item have?

learn: Conditionals choose a path. In Python: if temp > 30: print(“Hot”) elif temp > 15: print(“Mild”) else: print(“Cold”). Indentation shows which lines belong to each branch.

Loops repeat code. A for loop runs a set number of times: for i in range(5) runs with i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. A while loop repeats while a condition is true; make sure the condition eventually becomes false to avoid an infinite loop.
A procedure, or function, is a named block of reusable code: def area(w, h): return w * h. Parameters (w, h) receive arguments when called, as in area(3, 4), which returns 12.
Procedural abstraction lets you use a procedure without knowing its details, as long as you know its inputs and outputs. Breaking a program into procedures makes it easier to read, test and reuse.
units.try: Write a Python function that counts even numbers in a list, one line at a time with indentation: line 1, def count_evens(nums): line 2 (indented), count = 0 line 3, for n in nums: line 4 (indented more), if n % 2 == 0: line 5 (indented more), count = count + 1 line 6 (back at the level of line 2), return count. Test it on [3, 4, 7, 10, 12]; the answer should be 3.
check: How many times does for i in range(4) run?
Using a procedure by knowing its inputs and outputs, not its details
Writing everything in one long block

learn: An algorithm is a finite set of steps that solves a problem. All algorithms can be built from three structures: sequencing (steps in order), selection (choices) and iteration (repetition).

Linear search checks each item in turn and works on any list. Binary search works only on sorted lists: check the middle, then discard the half that cannot contain the target. For 1,000 items, binary search needs at most about 10 checks.

Efficiency describes how running time grows with input size. Algorithms that run in polynomial time are considered reasonable; those that take exponential time, like trying every combination, become impractical quickly.

Some problems are undecidable: no algorithm can always solve them. The halting problem, deciding whether any program will finish running, is the classic example. Heuristics give good-enough answers when exact ones are too slow.
units.try: Use binary search to find 37 in the sorted list 3, 8, 15, 22, 29, 37, 41, 50, 64. Step 1: middle is 29; 37 is larger, keep the right half (37, 41, 50, 64). Step 2: take 41 as the middle; 37 is smaller, keep 37. Step 3: check 37: found in three checks.
check: What are the three building blocks of algorithms?

learn: A simulation is a program that models a real-world process, such as weather, traffic or disease spread. Simulations let us test ideas safely, quickly and cheaply, but they rely on simplifying assumptions.
Random numbers add variety. In Python, import random, then random.randint(1, 6) returns a whole number from 1 to 6, simulating a die. Running a simulation many times shows likely outcomes.
As the number of trials grows, results usually approach theoretical probabilities. Flip a simulated coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads; flip it 10,000 times and you will likely get close to 50%.
Simulations have limits. If assumptions are wrong or data is biased, results can mislead. Good modelers state their assumptions and test results against real data.
units.try: Simulate rolling two dice 1,000 times (with code or by hand for 50 rolls). Count how often each total from 2 to 12 appears. Compare with theory: 7 should appear about 1/6 of the time, while 2 and 12 should each appear only about 1/36.
check: What happens to simulation results as the number of trials grows?
They stop changing after one trial

units.t: The Internet and How It Works
learn: The internet is a network of networks. Data is broken into packets, each with source and destination addresses. Packets may take different routes and arrive out of order, then are reassembled.

Protocols are agreed rules. IP (Internet Protocol) handles addressing; TCP ensures packets arrive completely and in order; UDP is faster but does not guarantee delivery, useful for live video. HTTP and HTTPS are used for web pages.
The Domain Name System (DNS) translates names into IP addresses, like a phone book. IPv4 addresses use 32 bits, about 4.3 billion addresses; IPv6 uses 128 bits to provide vastly more.

The internet is fault tolerant: redundancy means multiple paths exist, so if one connection fails, data can be rerouted. The World Wide Web is one service that runs on the internet, not the internet itself.
units.try: Act out packet switching with a friend. Write a sentence on paper, cut it into five numbered pieces, and pass them via different routes (different people or rooms). Have the receiver reassemble by number. Then remove one piece and discuss how TCP would request it again.
check: Translates domain names into IP addresses
Why is the internet fault tolerant?
Redundant paths let data reroute around failures

learn: Encryption scrambles data so only authorized people can read it. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key. Public key encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt, so strangers can communicate securely. HTTPS uses it.

Common threats include phishing (fake messages tricking you into giving information), malware (harmful software like viruses and ransomware) and weak passwords. A rogue access point is a fake Wi-Fi network that can capture data.
Defenses include strong unique passwords, multifactor authentication (something you know, have or are), software updates, antivirus tools and caution with links and attachments.

Personally identifiable information (PII), such as your name, address, birth date and Social Security number, can be used to steal your identity. Data collected by apps and websites can be combined to build detailed profiles, so review privacy settings.
units.try: Do a Caesar cipher by hand: shift each letter 3 forward. HELLO becomes KHOOR. Encrypt a short message for a friend and tell them the key. Then discuss why a computer could break this cipher instantly by trying all 25 shifts.
check: Fake messages that trick people into giving information
A way to speed up internet
In public key encryption, which key decrypts the message?

learn: Computing innovations bring benefits and harms. Social media connects people and spreads information quickly but can also spread misinformation and affect well-being. The same innovation can be used in ways its creators did not intend.

The digital divide is unequal access to computers and the internet, based on income, location or other factors. It affects education, jobs and access to services, and governments and groups work to close it.

Algorithms can carry bias if trained on biased data or designed without diverse input. For example, a hiring tool trained on past decisions could repeat unfair patterns. Testing with diverse data and teams helps.

Crowdsourcing uses many people to solve problems or gather data, as in citizen science projects. Creative Commons licenses and open source let creators share work legally. Respect copyright and give credit.
